fields.Front: List the five steps the slides use to build up the Internet's 'network of networks' structure.
fields.Back:
1) Connect every access ISP to every other: O(N^2) links, does not scale.
2) Connect each access ISP to one global transit ISP: customer-provider economic agreement.
3) Competing global ISPs (A, B, C) must interconnect: peering links and IXPs.
4) Regional ISPs arise to connect access nets to the large ISPs.
5) Content-provider networks (Google, Microsoft, Akamai) run private networks to bring content close to users.

fields.Front: Define peering link and IXP, and explain why they exist.
fields.Back:
Peering link: a direct connection between two ISPs (usually at the same level) so their traffic bypasses upstream providers; typically settlement-free (neither pays).
IXP (Internet exchange point): a third-party meeting point where many ISPs peer.
They exist because competing global/regional ISPs must interconnect so customers of different ISPs can communicate.

fields.Front: What are regional ISPs and tier-1 ISPs, who pays whom, and name tier-1 examples.
fields.Back:
Regional ISPs: connect access networks within a region to the large ISPs, adding a tier to the hierarchy.
Tier-1 ISPs: about a dozen large commercial ISPs with national/international coverage (Level 3, Sprint, AT&T, NTT); they peer with each other and pay no one for transit.
Money flows up: access ISP pays regional ISP, regional pays tier-1.

fields.Front: What is a content-provider network and why do Google, Microsoft or Akamai build one?
fields.Back:
A private global network connecting the provider's data centers to the Internet.
Why: brings services and content close to end users, and lets the provider bypass tier-1 and regional ISPs (saving transit fees, controlling performance) by peering directly with lower-tier ISPs or at IXPs.

fields.Front: What drove the evolution of the Internet's structure, and what do 'multi-homed' and 'settlement-free' mean?
fields.Back:
Evolution was driven by economics and national policies more than by performance.
Multi-homed: an ISP connects to two or more providers, staying connected if one fails.
Settlement-free: peering between ISPs at the same level in which neither party pays the other.

fields.Front: Textbook only: define PoP and multi-homing, and give the book's numbers for IXPs and content-provider bypass. (Kurose §1.3.3)
fields.Back:
PoP (point of presence): a group of one or more routers at a single location in a provider's network where customer ISPs can connect in. PoPs exist at every level except the bottom (access ISP) level; a customer typically leases a high-speed link from a third party to reach one.
Multi-homing: connecting to two or more provider ISPs. Any ISP except a tier-1 may do it, and the payoff is that it keeps sending and receiving packets even if one provider fails.
Numbers: there are over 600 IXPs (each typically a standalone building with its own switches); roughly a dozen tier-1 ISPs, though no group officially sanctions tier-1 status; and as of 2020 Amazon, Google, IBM and Microsoft could collectively reach 76% of the Internet without passing through a tier-1 ISP.

fields.Text: Connecting N access ISPs pairwise needs {{c1::O(N^2)}} links; instead each access ISP connects to a {{c1::global transit ISP}} under a {{c1::customer-provider}} economic agreement.

At the 'center' of the Internet: a small number of {{c1::tier-1 commercial ISPs}} (e.g., Level 3, Sprint, AT&T, NTT) and {{c1::content-provider networks}} (e.g., Google, Facebook) whose private networks connect their data centers, often {{c1::bypassing}} tier-1 and regional ISPs.
Internet hierarchy top to bottom: {{c1::tier-1 ISPs}}, {{c1::regional ISPs}}, {{c1::access ISPs}}; {{c1::IXPs}} provide peering points at each level, and content providers can connect at any level.
